summary.text: Judy Chu is the Democratic incumbent for California's 28th Congressional District, first elected to the U.S. House in a July 2009 special election. A professor with a doctorate in psychology who taught at Los Angeles-area community colleges, she held local and state offices in the San Gabriel Valley, including three terms as mayor of Monterey Park, before entering Congress as the first Chinese American woman elected to the House. She serves on the Ways and Means and Budget committees.

paragraphs.text: Chu was born in Los Angeles on July 7, 1953.

She earned a bachelor's degree from UCLA in 1974 and a Ph.D. from the California School of Professional Psychology in 1979, and she worked as a professor at Los Angeles City College and East Los Angeles College.
She was first elected to the Garvey School District Board of Education in 1985, and in 1988 she won a seat on the Monterey Park City Council, where she served as mayor three times.
Chu served in the California State Assembly, representing the 49th District, from 2001 to 2006, and was then elected to the State Board of Equalization, California's elected tax board.
She won a July 2009 special election to the U.S. House, becoming the first Chinese American woman elected to Congress.

In the House, Chu serves on the Ways and Means Committee, where she is a member of its Health, Worker and Family Support, and Oversight subcommittees, and on the Budget Committee; she is also a member of the House Democratic Caucus Steering and Policy Committee.
She was elected chair of the Congressional Asian Pacific American Caucus in 2011 and served in that role until 2025, and she founded and co-chairs the Congressional Creative Rights Caucus.

Her official biography lists among her accomplishments a congressional resolution of regret for the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882, the designation of the San Gabriel Mountains as a national monument, and a requirement that the Department of Defense address military hazing.
According to that biography, she lives in Monterey Park with her husband, Michael Eng, and they have been residents there for over 30 years.
